## Personality

Calm, practical and gently teasing. She has seen every kind of injury a ship can cause and is unimpressed by most of them.

## Lore

Clemence is the harbour healer, and her door on the Waterfront is the one people knock on when a rope has taken the skin off their palms, a hook has gone where a hook should not go, or a crate has landed on a foot. She is fifty-two, calm, practical and gently teasing, and she has seen every kind of injury a ship can cause. Most of them do not impress her. Sailors who come in white-faced and groaning are told, kindly, that they will live, and that they should have worn gloves.

### The healer's house

Clemence was born in the narrow house where she still works, a few doors from the Salt and Bread, with bunches of herbs hanging from every beam and a smell of camphor that clings to the curtains. Her mother, Tressa, was the harbour healer before her, and Clemence grew up rolling bandages, grinding salves and holding the lamp while her mother stitched. When Tressa died twenty-two years ago, Clemence was thirty and had been doing half the work already. Nobody asked who the new healer was. They simply kept knocking.

She never married. She says she has enough people relying on her as it is. Her house has a front door for ordinary trouble and a back door onto the alley for people who would rather not be seen coming in, and she keeps both doors' secrets equally.

She sells salves, bandages and seasickness tonic. The tonic is her mother's recipe, made with ginger and peppermint, and she buys the ginger from Marisol on Merchant Street. Lately Marisol's ginger has come in late, and twice this spring Clemence has had to make the tonic weaker than she likes.

### Ysolde

Her closest friend is Ysolde, the Keeper of the Light. The friendship began sixteen years ago, on the day Ysolde's husband Kenver died suddenly while mending his nets on the fish market steps. Wenna, who was mending beside him, sent a boy running for Clemence, and there was nothing to be done. Clemence was the one who climbed the lighthouse stairs to tell Ysolde. Ysolde listened, nodded, and then went up and lit the lamp, because ships were out. Clemence stayed with her at the top of the tower until the morning, and has been climbing those hundred and seventeen stairs ever since.

These days she goes up once a week with a salve for Ysolde's knees, and the two of them drink tea at the top of the tower and agree about almost everyone in Bain Harbour. Clemence is the only visitor Ysolde invites, and she knows it. She does not know about the pale lights her friend has seen under the water. Ysolde has never mentioned them, and Clemence, who notices most things, has noticed only that Ysolde looks out past the headland a little longer than she used to.

### The back door

Her most regular back-door patient is Keziah, the young sword for hire who sails with Captain Seraphine. Before every voyage of the Bright Morrow, Keziah knocks at dawn for a bottle of seasickness tonic, and Clemence hands it over with a remark about sailors who cannot keep their breakfast down. She has never told anyone, and she never will. She teases Keziah only gently, because she thinks the girl is braver than half the captains in the harbour for going to sea at all.

### The notes

Lately Clemence has been treating injuries she cannot explain. A deckhand came in with a row of round welts across his forearm, each the size of a coin, from something he never saw. A dockworker had a long, shallow scrape down his calf, too straight for a rock and too clean for a hook. Twice there have been stings that matched no jellyfish she knows, and she knows them all. Clemence writes each one down in a casebook: the date, the patient, the ship, the wound, and what the patient said happened, which is rarely the same as what she thinks happened.

She has not shown the casebook to anyone. She suspects others in the harbour are keeping notes of their own, and she has begun to wonder what would happen if they were laid side by side.

### What she wants and fears

Clemence wants to understand what she is treating, because she cannot treat properly what she cannot name. She fears the day someone is carried to her door with a wound she cannot close.

### Hooks

A quest could bring Clemence ginger from a cargo that never arrived, find the creature that left a row of coin-sized welts on a deckhand's arm, or carry her casebook to someone else who has been writing things down.
